title: Electric Utility
fit_question: Tell me about a time when you had to convince leadership of your idea. Tell me about a time when you had to work under tight timelines.
prompt: GPE operates ten coal-fired electricity plants in the United States. It sources coal partly from its own mines and partly from third parties, and its profitability from coal-generated electricity has recently declined. Diagnose the causes and recommend a response.

clarifying_info.answer: GPE serves more than one million customers through wholesalers in deregulated markets; demand grows about 3% annually and the market is fragmented.
Competitive forces set one annual electricity price for all customers, and current supply meets demand.
GPE leases regulated transmission lines; for simplicity, coal is the main variable cost.

interviewer_notes: Qualitative interviewer-led Round 2 case. Require structured brainstorming and repeatedly ask 'what else?' The intended diagnosis is cost inflation rather than revenue weakness. The coal-mine discussion hinges on opportunity cost and supply security, not the mine's 30% internal discount alone.

suggested_framework.summary: Confirm whether revenue or cost explains the decline, then examine coal acquisition, generation and transmission.

stages.interviewer_asks: What could be causing the profitability decline?
stages.expected_answer: Split profit into price, volume, fixed and variable costs. Since market price is competitively set and demand is growing, prioritize costs across coal acquisition, electricity generation and transmission while checking customer shifts and alternative generation.
good_answer_signals: Prioritizes costs based on market facts

stages.interviewer_asks: What issues could arise in acquiring coal, generating electricity and transmitting it?
stages.expected_answer: Coal: transport mode and distance, source quality variation, geographic disruption, union labor and supplier terms. Generation: old equipment, operating inconsistency across ten plants, labor scarcity and environmental regulation. Transmission: distance to customers, lease-sharing contracts, line losses and peak-hour charges.
good_answer_signals: Produces at least three specific issues per step
Organizes ideas along the supply chain

stages.interviewer_asks: GPE's own mine provides coal at a 30% lower internal rate than third parties, and coal can be sold broadly at the market price. Should GPE keep the mine?
stages.expected_answer: The internal discount is not an economic advantage by itself because using the coal sacrifices a sale at the market price. Keep the mine if supply security, quality control, reduced supplier power, diversification and risk reduction exceed ownership costs and the value available from selling or divesting it.
good_answer_signals: Identifies strategic benefits of vertical integration

stages.interviewer_asks: GPE averages 80% utilization versus a 77% industry average. Should it target 90%?
stages.expected_answer: Not automatically. Electricity demand is cyclical and capacity must cover peaks, so average utilization below 100% provides reliability reserve. At 80%, GPE already exceeds the industry benchmark; test peak requirements, outage reserve and marginal economics before raising the target.
good_answer_signals: Rejects a target based only on a higher percentage

stages.expected_answer: Prioritize cost reduction across coal transport and sourcing, plant efficiency and transmission contracts and losses. Retain the mine for supply and quality control if those benefits exceed ownership costs, and do not force utilization to 90% without a peak-demand reliability study. Rank the top five savings opportunities and build an implementation plan.

synthesis: GPE's likely issue is rising cost, not weak demand or pricing. Diagnose coal transport, supplier and labor costs; plant age, operating variation and regulation; and transmission leases and losses. Retain the mine only for real supply-security, quality-control and diversification value after opportunity cost, and keep utilization near 80% unless a peak-demand study shows 90% is reliable and economic.
what_great_looks_like: Generates concrete ideas across all three supply-chain steps
Applies opportunity cost to the mine
Explains why spare capacity can be valuable
common_pitfalls: Searches for price growth despite competitive pricing
Treats the mine's transfer price as true savings
Assumes higher utilization is always better

extraction.notes: The case has no candidate exhibits or numerical calculation. The source's coal-mine scenario wording is internally awkward; the economic interpretation is a make-versus-buy decision with market-value opportunity cost. Reviewed and accepted by Claude 2026-09-30.
